newsitem.title: UK: Job fears hit British consumer confidence - survey.
newsitem.headline: Job fears hit British consumer confidence - survey.

text.p: A recent dip in British consumer confidence and expected borrowing has more to do with job and earnings insecurity than the prospect of a change of government at the election, a new survey said on Tuesday.

Fears over jobs and earnings have deterred consumers from borrowing more this quarter and helped reverse last quarter's rise in confidence, the Hamilton Direct Bank said in its new "Consumer Confidence Bulletin".

The survey found 22 percent of individuals are less confident about borrowing this quarter, with only 14 percent more confident. This negative balance of eight percent compares with a positive balance of seven percent quoted in the last quarter.

"The majority of those whose borrowing intentions had deteriorated said their reduced level of confidence in the economy has not been affected by the prospect of a general election, regardless of the outcome," the survey said.

The election is due to be held by May and, if the opinion polls are right, the opposition Labour Party will win. "You might expect a run-up to the general election to cause reduced confidence," said Barry Moore, a spokesman for Public & Corporate Economic Consultants (PACEC), the independent economics and strategy consultancy which carried out the research.
"But, interestingly, income stability and job security were the main factors cited, rather than which party will be in power."
Hamilton Direct Bank is a division of HFC Bank, part of Household International, the biggest consumer finance group in the U.S.
